content: Nedocromil sodium and sodium cromoglycate, when inhaled shortly before exercise, both appear to mitigate the severity of exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB). However, there is ongoing debate regarding which of the two medications is more effective in this context. The purpose of this review was to directly compare the effects of prophylactic doses of nedocromil sodium (NCS) and sodium cromoglycate (SCG) on lung function following exercise in individuals diagnosed with EIB. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that met specific criteria: participants were aged six years or older, had a confirmed diagnosis of asthma with EIB, underwent an exercise challenge sufficient to provoke bronchoconstriction, and had lung function outcomes reported as changes in forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) or peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR). To identify relevant studies, the Cochrane Airways Review Group Asthma Register was searched, along with bibliographies of related studies and review articles. Primary authors, content experts, and drug manufacturers were also contacted for additional data. No language restrictions were applied, and the search was current as of December 2007. Nine studies involving a total of 162 participants were included in the review. Data extraction and quality assessments were performed independently by two reviewers using standardized forms and validated criteria. In some cases, data were extrapolated from graphs. Results from similar studies were pooled and analyzed using a random-effects model, with outcomes reported as weighted mean differences (WMD) or odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The analysis revealed no significant difference between NCS and SCG in terms of the maximum percentage decrease in FEV1 following exercise (WMD = -0.88; 95% CI: -4.50 to 2.74). Similarly, there was no significant difference in the likelihood of achieving complete protection (defined as a maximum FEV1 fall of less than 10%; OR = 0.95; 95% CI: 0.50 to 1.80) or clinical protection (defined as less than a 50% improvement over placebo; OR = 0.71; 95% CI: 0.36 to 1.39). Additionally, there were no significant differences in the incidence of side effects such as unpleasant taste (OR = 6.85; 95% CI: 0.77 to 60.73) or sore throat (OR = 3.46; 95% CI: 0.32 to 37.48). No statistically significant heterogeneity was observed in these pooled comparisons. Subgroup analyses, which considered factors such as age, medication dosage, and the timing of exercise after inhalation, were consistent with the overall findings. In conclusion, there were no significant differences between nedocromil sodium and sodium cromoglycate in their effects on pulmonary function during the immediate post-exercise period in both adults and children with EIB. This includes outcomes such as the maximum percentage decrease in FEV1, the likelihood of achieving complete or clinical protection, and the occurrence of side effects.
